name: Peking Duck
description: Roast duck from Beijing prepared since the imperial era, prized for its thin, crispy skin, which the cook slices in front of diners. It is the best-known dish of Beijing cuisine.
how_to_eat: Roll slices of skin and meat in thin pancakes with spring onion, cucumber and sweet bean sauce.
how_to_order: Order a whole or half duck at a roast-duck restaurant; it is carved at the table.

name: Zhajiangmian
description: Thick wheat noodles topped with zhajiang, a fried sauce of fermented soybean paste and minced pork. Shredded fresh vegetables such as cucumber are added on top.
how_to_eat: Mix the sauce and vegetables through the noodles before eating.
how_to_order: Ask for 'zhajiangmian' at Beijing noodle shops.

name: Jiaozi
description: Chinese dumplings of ground meat or vegetable filling sealed in thin dough, then boiled, steamed or pan-fried. They are a major Chinese New Year dish across northern China and eaten all year in the north.
how_to_eat: Dip in black vinegar and soy sauce.
how_to_order: Order by weight or by the plate at dumpling houses, choosing the filling.

name: Jianbing
description: A crepe-like breakfast of wheat and grain batter spread on a hotplate and cooked with egg, sauces, scallions and coriander, often wrapped around a crisp cracker or youtiao. It is one of China's most popular street breakfasts.
how_to_eat: Eat folded and hot from the street cart.
how_to_order: Buy from morning street carts; say if you want chilli sauce.

name: Instant-boiled Mutton (Shuan Yangrou)
description: A Beijing hot pot in which thin slices of mutton are dipped briefly in boiling water or broth at the table. Traditionally a winter dish, it is now eaten year-round.
how_to_eat: Swish each slice in the pot for a few seconds, then dip in sesame sauce.
how_to_order: Order mutton slices by the plate at a Beijing-style hot pot restaurant.

name: Tanghulu
description: Chinese hawthorn fruits on a bamboo skewer coated in hardened sugar syrup. Made since the Song dynasty, it is a classic winter snack of northern China.
how_to_eat: Bite the crunchy sugar shell and fruit straight off the skewer.
how_to_order: Buy a skewer from street vendors, mostly in winter.

name: Douzhi
description: A grey, slightly sour fermented mung bean drink made as a by-product of cellophane noodle production. It has a recorded history of over 300 years and is a famously divisive Beijing taste.
how_to_eat: Sip hot, traditionally with pickles and fried dough rings.
how_to_order: Ask for 'douzhi' at old Beijing snack shops.

name: Lüdagun
description: A rolled glutinous rice pastry filled with red bean paste and coated in yellow soybean flour. Of Manchu origin, it became a famous Beijing snack; its name means 'rolling donkey'.
how_to_eat: Eat in slices at room temperature.
how_to_order: Buy at traditional Beijing snack shops.

name: Mapo Tofu
description: Tofu in a spicy, oily red sauce of douban chilli bean paste and fermented black beans, with minced meat, traditionally beef. It likely originated at a Chengdu restaurant in the 1860s-1870s.
how_to_eat: Spoon over steamed rice.
how_to_order: Ask for 'mapo doufu' at any Sichuan restaurant.

name: Kung Pao Chicken
description: Stir-fried cubes of chicken with peanuts, vegetables, dried chillies and Sichuan peppercorns. It comes from Sichuan cuisine and has spread across China in many milder variations.
how_to_eat: Eat with steamed rice.
how_to_order: Ask for 'gongbao jiding' at Sichuan restaurants.

name: Dandan Noodles
description: Wheat noodles in a spicy sauce of chilli oil, Sichuan pepper, preserved vegetables and minced pork, topped with scallions and peanuts. In Chengdu it is served dry rather than as a soup.
how_to_eat: Toss the noodles thoroughly to coat them in the sauce at the bottom of the bowl.
how_to_order: Order a small bowl at Chengdu noodle shops.

name: Twice-cooked Pork
description: Pork belly that is simmered, sliced and then stir-fried again with garlic sprouts or leeks and chilli bean paste. The name means 'meat returned to the wok'.
how_to_eat: Eat with steamed rice.
how_to_order: Ask for 'huiguorou' at Sichuan restaurants.

name: Fuqi Feipian
description: A cold Sichuan dish of thinly sliced beef and beef offal such as heart, tongue and tripe, dressed in chilli oil and Sichuan pepper. It should taste both spicy and mouth-numbing; real lung is rarely used despite the name.
how_to_eat: Eat cold as a starter with other dishes.
how_to_order: Order as a cold appetiser at Sichuan restaurants.

name: Chongqing Hot Pot
description: A spicy, numbing (mala) hot pot in which diners cook meats, offal, vegetables and tofu in a simmering broth loaded with chillies and Sichuan pepper. It is the signature meal of Chongqing.
how_to_eat: Cook items in the broth yourself, then dip in sesame oil with garlic.
how_to_order: Choose spicy, mild or a split (yuanyang) pot at a hot pot restaurant, then tick ingredients on the menu.

name: Har Gow
description: Cantonese dim sum dumplings of shrimp steamed in a wrapper that turns translucent when cooked, hence the name crystal shrimp dumplings. They are a benchmark of a dim sum kitchen's skill.
how_to_eat: Eat whole or in two bites, with tea.
how_to_order: Order a basket at a dim sum (yum cha) restaurant in the morning.

name: Siu Mai
description: Open-topped steamed dumplings of ground pork, often with shrimp, served as Cantonese dim sum. They are one of the most common dim sum dishes.
how_to_eat: Eat with soy sauce or chilli oil.
how_to_order: Order a basket at a dim sum restaurant.

name: Char Siu
description: Cantonese barbecued pork, usually boneless shoulder marinated in hoisin, soy sauce, Chinese wine and five-spice and glazed with maltose or honey while roasting. It is a staple of Cantonese roast-meat shops.
how_to_eat: Eat sliced over rice or noodles.
how_to_order: Order by weight or as a rice plate at a siu mei (roast meat) shop.

name: Cheung Fun (Rice Noodle Roll)
description: Thin steamed sheets of rice noodle rolled around shrimp, beef or other fillings and doused with seasoned soy sauce. It originated in Guangdong and is served as dim sum or a breakfast snack.
how_to_eat: Eat with chopsticks while hot, with the soy sauce.
how_to_order: Order at dim sum restaurants or breakfast stalls, choosing shrimp or beef.

name: Wonton Noodles
description: Thin egg noodles in hot broth with shrimp wonton dumplings and leafy greens such as gai lan. It is a classic Cantonese noodle dish.
how_to_eat: Eat the wontons and noodles, then sip the broth.
how_to_order: Ask for 'wonton mein' at Cantonese noodle shops.

name: Egg Tart
description: A pastry crust filled with egg custard, derived from the English custard tart and Portuguese pastel de nata. It is sold at dim sum restaurants, Chinese bakeries and Hong Kong-style cafes.
how_to_eat: Eat warm, fresh from the oven.
how_to_order: Buy from Cantonese bakeries or order at dim sum.

name: Cantonese Roast Goose
description: Goose roasted until the skin is crisp and glossy, a centrepiece of Cantonese roast meat (siu mei) cooking.
how_to_eat: Eat with plum sauce, over rice or on its own.
how_to_order: Order by the quarter or half at a siu mei shop.

name: Xiaolongbao
description: Small soup dumplings filled with pork and jellied stock, steamed in a little bamboo basket (xiaolong). They are generally believed to come from Shanghai.
how_to_eat: Bite a small hole, sip the soup, then eat with vinegar and ginger.
how_to_order: Order a basket (usually 6-10) at a dumpling house.

name: Shengjian Mantou
description: Small pan-fried buns filled with pork and gelatin that melts into soup, with a crisp base. In Shanghai they have thin skins and are a breakfast favourite.
how_to_eat: Bite carefully as the soup inside is very hot.
how_to_order: Order by the portion (usually four) at shengjian shops.

name: Shanghai Hairy Crab
description: The Chinese mitten crab, a freshwater crab with furry claws, steamed and prized for its rich roe. It is a famous seasonal delicacy of Shanghai and the lower Yangtze.
how_to_eat: Crack the shell and dip the meat in ginger vinegar.
how_to_order: Look for it in autumn at Shanghai restaurants and markets.

name: Lion's Head Meatballs
description: Large pork meatballs stewed with napa cabbage (white style) or in soy sauce (red style). It comes from the Huaiyang cuisine of eastern China.
how_to_eat: Break the meatball with a spoon and eat with the broth and cabbage.
how_to_order: Order at Huaiyang or Shanghainese restaurants.

name: Yangzhou Fried Rice
description: Egg fried rice with mixed vegetables and two proteins, typically pork and shrimp, with scallions. It is one of China's best-known wok-fried rice dishes.
how_to_eat: Eat as a main dish or alongside others.
how_to_order: Ask for 'Yangzhou chaofan' at Chinese restaurants.

name: Dongpo Pork
description: Thick squares of pork belly pan-fried and then red-braised in wine and soy sauce until tender. The Hangzhou dish is named after the Song-dynasty poet Su Dongpo.
how_to_eat: Eat in small bites with steamed rice.
how_to_order: Order at Hangzhou restaurants, usually by the piece.

name: West Lake Fish in Vinegar Gravy
description: Grass carp poached and covered in a glossy sweet-and-sour vinegar sauce. A Hangzhou specialty dating to the Southern Song dynasty.
how_to_eat: Share the whole fish, eating the flesh with the sauce.
how_to_order: Order at Hangzhou restaurants around West Lake.

name: Longjing Tea
description: A pan-roasted green tea with flat, hand-shaped leaves from around Longjing Village near West Lake, Hangzhou. It is one of China's Famous Teas, and Longjing cha is a Protected Designation of Origin in the EU and UK.
how_to_eat: Brew in a glass with hot (not boiling) water and watch the leaves unfurl.
how_to_order: Order at teahouses in Hangzhou; spring 'pre-Qingming' tea is the most prized.

name: Mao's Red Braised Pork
description: Pork belly red-braised until soft and glossy; the Hunan version is said to be one of Mao Zedong's favourite dishes. The Hunan provincial government has even codified the recipe.
how_to_eat: Eat with steamed rice.
how_to_order: Ask for 'Mao shi hongshaorou' at Hunan restaurants.

name: Changsha Stinky Tofu
description: Black, fermented tofu deep-fried and served with chilli sauce, a traditional snack of Changsha. It is one of the 'Three Treasures of Hunan'; the brine is traditionally made with vegetables and meat.
how_to_eat: Eat hot from the stall with the chilli dressing.
how_to_order: Buy from night-market stalls in Changsha.

name: Steamed Fish Head with Chopped Chillies
description: A large fish head, traditionally bighead carp, steamed under a thick layer of fermented chopped red chillies (duojiao) with garlic and ginger. It is the most famous duojiao dish and a representative of Hunan cuisine.
how_to_eat: Eat the fish and use the sauce with rice or noodles.
how_to_order: Order at Hunan restaurants; ask for noodles to mix into the leftover sauce.

name: Hot Dry Noodles (Reganmian)
description: Noodles served without broth, tossed in sesame paste and seasonings. It is the most famous breakfast food of Wuhan, sold by street carts and restaurants.
how_to_eat: Mix well so the sesame paste coats every strand.
how_to_order: Buy for breakfast at Wuhan noodle stalls.

name: Roujiamo
description: A Shaanxi street food of chopped braised meat stuffed into a flatbread, sometimes called the Chinese hamburger.
how_to_eat: Eat hand-held while warm.
how_to_order: Buy from street stalls in Xi'an, including the Muslim Quarter (beef or lamb there).

name: Biangbiang Noodles
description: Very thick, long, belt-like hand-pulled wheat noodles from Shaanxi, often dressed with chilli and hot oil. They are one of the 'Eight Curiosities of Shaanxi' and famous for their hugely complex written character.
how_to_eat: Toss the noodles in the oil and chilli before eating.
how_to_order: Order at Xi'an noodle shops.

name: Yangrou Paomo
description: A hot lamb soup with pieces of baked wheat flatbread (mo) cooked in it. It is a popular specialty of Xi'an and Shaanxi.
how_to_eat: Traditionally you break the bread into small pieces yourself before it goes into the soup.
how_to_order: Order at Xi'an paomo restaurants, where you are handed bread to tear.

name: Liangpi
description: Cold, chewy noodles of wheat or rice flour, dressed with chilli oil and vinegar. A specialty originating in Xi'an that has spread throughout China.
how_to_eat: Eat cold, mixed with the sauce.
how_to_order: Buy from noodle stalls and street vendors in Xi'an.

name: Lanzhou Beef Noodles
description: Hand-pulled noodles in clear beef broth, closely associated with Hui Muslim cuisine. By 2015 there were about 50,000 shops serving it across China.
how_to_eat: Eat with the chilli oil and radish slices in the broth.
how_to_order: Choose your noodle thickness when ordering at a Lanzhou lamian shop.

name: Chuanr (Lamb Skewers)
description: Small pieces of meat, classically lamb, roasted on skewers and seasoned with cumin and chilli. It originated in Xinjiang's Uyghur cuisine and is now a street food across China.
how_to_eat: Eat straight from the skewer.
how_to_order: Order by the skewer at street grills and night markets.

name: Dapanji (Big Plate Chicken)
description: A spicy stew of chicken and potatoes with peppers, invented in Shawan, Xinjiang in the 1980s. It is served halal and is popular across the region.
how_to_eat: Share it, then mix the leftover sauce with the wide noodles served at the end.
how_to_order: Order a large plate to share at Xinjiang restaurants.

name: Laghman
description: Hand-pulled noodles topped with a stir-fry of meat and vegetables, a signature of Uyghur cuisine.
how_to_eat: Mix the topping through the noodles.
how_to_order: Order at Uyghur restaurants.

name: Polo (Uyghur Pilaf)
description: Rice cooked with fried mutton or chicken, onions and sliced carrots, sometimes with raisins and dried apricots. It is a signature Uyghur dish, traditionally eaten by hand.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand or with a spoon, often with salad.
how_to_order: Ask for 'polo' or 'zhuafan' at Uyghur restaurants.

name: Samsa (Kao Baozi)
description: Hand-held lamb pies roasted in a tunur (clay oven). They are a common Uyghur filled bread.
how_to_eat: Eat hot from the oven.
how_to_order: Buy from bakers with a tunur at Uyghur markets.

name: Crossing-the-bridge Noodles
description: A rice noodle soup in which raw ingredients and noodles are added to a very hot broth at the table. It is one of the best-known dishes of Yunnan cuisine.
how_to_eat: Add the meats first, then the vegetables and noodles, to cook in the hot broth.
how_to_order: Order at Yunnan noodle restaurants; set sizes come with more toppings.

name: Erkuai
description: A rice cake particular to Yunnan, sold grilled, fried or sliced into dishes.
how_to_eat: Eat grilled and folded around fillings, or stir-fried.
how_to_order: Buy grilled erkuai from street vendors in Yunnan.

name: Pu'er Tea
description: A fermented tea made from Yunnan large-leaf tea plants, often pressed into cakes and aged. Pu'er Cha is a Chinese geographical indication and is protected in the EU under the EU-China GI agreement.
how_to_eat: Rinse the leaves once, then steep repeatedly in small cups.
how_to_order: Order at teahouses or buy cakes at tea markets in Yunnan.

name: Maotai
description: A style of baijiu (Chinese grain liquor) from the town of Maotai in Guizhou, made from sorghum and a wheat-based starter. It has a nutty, savoury aroma and is China's most prestigious spirit.
how_to_eat: Sip in small glasses, usually as toasts during a banquet.
how_to_order: Order by the bottle in restaurants; it is expensive.
